1.1: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: ‘anuśāsana’ means teaching handed down, not invented; SK 69–71 says the same of Sāṃkhya, received from Kapila through Āsuri and Pañcaśikha. Yoga is the practice of what Sāṃkhya analyses. Veda: the word yoga first appears for the mind in Ṛgveda 5.81.1 — ‘the seers yoke (yuñjate) their mind and yoke their thoughts’ — echoed in Śvetāśvatara Up. 2.1. Meaning: the Veda already treated the mind as something to be harnessed; this text sets out how.
1.2: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: the citta is Sāṃkhya’s inner instrument — buddhi, ahaṃkāra and manas (SK 33, 35). Stilling its movements is the practical form of SK 64’s knowledge. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 2.3.10–11 — ‘when the five senses rest with the mind and the intellect does not stir, that is the highest state; this steady holding of the senses they call yoga.’ Maitrī Up. 6.34: ‘mind alone is the cause of bondage and release.’ Meaning: freedom is not won by adding anything, but by stilling what moves.
1.3: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 65 describes the freed puruṣa ‘abiding in itself (svastha), like a spectator’ — the same picture as ‘the seer abides in its own nature’. Veda: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 4.4.23 — ‘calm, restrained, withdrawn, patient and collected (samāhita), he sees the Self in the self.’ Meaning: when the mind is still, nothing new appears; what was always there stops being hidden.
1.4: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 20 — through contact with puruṣa the unconscious intellect seems conscious, and puruṣa seems to act. This ‘taking the form of the vṛttis’ is that mutual borrowing. Veda: Muṇḍaka Up. 3.1.2 — the self on the same tree, sunk in confusion, grieves, deluded by its own helplessness. Meaning: in ordinary life we take ourselves to be whatever passes through the mind.
1.5: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 23 divides buddhi’s states into sattvic (virtue, knowledge, dispassion, power) and tamasic; Yoga’s ‘afflicted / unafflicted’ vṛttis follow the same line — thoughts that bind and thoughts that free. Veda: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 1.3.28 — ‘lead me from the unreal to the real, from darkness to light.’ Meaning: some thoughts are themselves the way out; practice begins by using them against the rest.
1.6: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: the five vṛttis are buddhi’s functions; SK 23 calls buddhi ‘adhyavasāya’, ascertainment, and these five are the ways it ascertains, rightly or wrongly. Veda: Chāndogya Up. 6.1.4 — clay is real, ‘the modification is only a name arising from speech’ — distinguishes true knowledge from naming. Meaning: everything we know arrives through one of five doors; knowing the doors is the first step to closing them.
1.7: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: identical to SK 4–5 — perception, inference and reliable testimony are the only three means of knowledge. Veda: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 2.4.5 — the Self ‘is to be seen, heard, reflected on and meditated upon’: hearing (testimony), reflection (inference) and direct seeing. Meaning: Yoga and Sāṃkhya share one theory of knowledge, and the Upaniṣad already ranks direct seeing above hearsay.
1.8: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 44 and 47 call this viparyaya, error, and make it the root of bondage; it is the same word Patañjali uses here. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 1.2.5 — ‘dwelling in ignorance, thinking themselves wise, the deluded go round like the blind led by the blind.’ Meaning: the trouble is not lack of experience but experience misread.
1.9: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: vikalpa — thought carried by words alone — is why SK 64’s liberating insight is phrased as the negation ‘I am not, nothing is mine’ rather than a new concept. Veda: Taittirīya Up. 2.4 — ‘from which words turn back, with the mind, not reaching it’; Ṛgveda 10.71.4 — ‘one who looks has not seen speech.’ Meaning: language can point, but it can also build things that are not there.
1.10: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: sleep is a tamasic state of buddhi (SK 13: tamas is heavy and covering). Yoga insists it is still a vṛtti — something is experienced, namely absence. Veda: Māṇḍūkya Up. 5 — deep sleep is ‘a mass of knowing, made of bliss’, and the fourth (turīya) lies beyond it; Praśna Up. 4.2 — in sleep the senses merge into mind like rays into the setting sun. Meaning: the Self is not found in blankness; it is the witness of the blankness.
1.11: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: memory rides on saṃskāra, the residue SK 67 compares to a potter’s wheel still turning. Veda: Chāndogya Up. 7.26.2 — ‘when the sattva is pure, memory becomes firm; with firm memory, all knots are released.’ Meaning: memory binds when it replays the past, and frees when it holds the truth steady.
1.12: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 64 — liberating knowledge arises ‘from the practice of the principles’ (tattvābhyāsa); SK 23 lists dispassion (virāga) among buddhi’s sattvic forms. Practice and dispassion are the two halves of that. Veda: Muṇḍaka Up. 1.2.12 — having examined the worlds won by action, the seeker ‘should arrive at dispassion: the uncreated is not gained by the created.’ Smṛti: Gītā 6.35 repeats the pair — ‘by practice and dispassion the mind is held.’ Meaning: one hand steadies, the other lets go.
1.13: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: ‘sthiti’, stability, is the tamas-like steadiness SK 13 assigns to the guṇas, now turned to use. Veda: Taittirīya Up. 1.11 — ‘do not be careless about study (svādhyāyān mā pramadaḥ)’; Kaṭha Up. 2.3.11 — yoga ‘arises and passes away’, so it must be held. Meaning: steadiness is not a gift; it is a repeated effort.
1.14: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 64 speaks of ‘tattvābhyāsa’, practice of the principles — knowledge in Sāṃkhya is also not one reading but a ripening. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 1.3.14 — ‘arise, awake, approach the great ones and learn; the path is like a razor’s edge.’ Meaning: long, unbroken and sincere — the Upaniṣad’s razor’s edge in three words.
1.15: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 2 rejects both seen and scriptural (ānuśravika) means — the very two kinds of object named here, ‘seen and heard of’. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 1.1.26–28 — Naciketas refuses Yama’s gifts of wealth, long life and pleasures: ‘they wear out the vigour of the senses; keep your horses and your songs.’ Meaning: the Veda’s own heaven is counted as one more object to want.
1.16: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: this is SK 66 in seed form — once the puruṣa is seen, the guṇas lose their pull: ‘I have seen her,’ and he becomes indifferent. Veda: Śvetāśvatara Up. 4.5 — the unborn one leaves the red-white-black she-goat (prakṛti, the guṇas) ‘having enjoyed her’; Gītā 2.59 — even the taste (rasa) falls away on seeing the Highest. Meaning: lower dispassion is restraint; higher dispassion is simply no longer interested.
1.17: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: the four stages climb Sāṃkhya’s ladder in reverse — gross elements, subtle elements, the sattvic senses, and asmitā/ahaṃkāra (SK 22, 24–25). Veda: Taittirīya Up. 2.1–5 lists five sheaths, from food to bliss, each subtler; Kaṭha Up. 1.3.10–11 orders objects, mind, intellect, the great self, the unmanifest, puruṣa. Meaning: meditation moves inward along the same map creation moved outward.
1.18: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: only saṃskāras remain — SK 67’s ‘wheel still turning from its impetus’. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 1.3.13 — merge speech into mind, mind into the knowing self, that into the great self, and that into the peaceful Self. Meaning: the last step is not another object but the stopping of objects.
1.19: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 45 says outright, ‘from dispassion comes absorption into prakṛti (prakṛtilaya)’ — a high state, but not liberation. Patañjali uses the same word. Veda: Chāndogya Up. 5.10 contrasts paths that return with one that does not; Muṇḍaka Up. 1.2.10 — those who think ritual merit the highest ‘enjoy heaven, then re-enter this world.’ Meaning: even very refined states can be one more place to get stuck.
1.20: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 51’s siddhis — reasoning, instruction, study, friends — are Sāṃkhya’s version of these supports. Veda: Taittirīya Up. 2.4 — the knowing self has ‘faith (śraddhā) for its head … yoga for its trunk’; Kaṭha Up. 1.1.2 — śraddhā enters the boy Naciketas before his quest. Meaning: the Veda puts faith first, and Patañjali agrees — but faith that is then tested by vigour and wisdom.
1.21: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 1 — inquiry begins because suffering strikes (abhighāta); intensity of the blow sets the urgency. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 1.3.14 — ‘arise, awake’; Chāndogya Up. 7.1.3 — Nārada: ‘I know the mantras but not the Self … I am in sorrow; take me across.’ Meaning: the speed of the journey matches the honesty of the need.
1.22: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 54 grades beings by sattva, rajas and tamas; practitioners are likewise graded. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 1.2.1–2 — the wise choose the good (śreyas) over the pleasant (preyas), the dull choose comfort. Meaning: the same practice, held with different intensity, gives different results.
1.23: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: here Yoga adds what classical Sāṃkhya leaves out. The Kārikā has no Īśvara; SK 57 argues prakṛti works unaided, like milk for the calf. Veda: Śvetāśvatara Up. 6.13 names ‘that cause, to be reached by Sāṃkhya and Yoga’, and 6.11 calls the one God ‘witness, pure, alone, without guṇas’. Meaning: the Upaniṣad keeps the Lord the Kārikā drops, and Yoga follows the Upaniṣad.
1.24: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: Īśvara is ‘a special puruṣa’ — still Sāṃkhya’s category of consciousness (SK 17–19), only never bound. Veda: Śvetāśvatara Up. 6.11 — ‘one God hidden in all beings … the witness, pure consciousness, alone, without qualities’; Chāndogya Up. 8.7.1 — the Self is ‘free of evil, ageing, death and sorrow.’ Meaning: the ideal the yogi moves toward is already real in one puruṣa.
1.25: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: Vyāsa, commenting here, quotes Pañcaśikha: the first knower, out of compassion, taught the doctrine to Āsuri — the same lineage SK 70 gives. Veda: Śvetāśvatara Up. 5.2 — the One ‘who bore the seer Kapila with knowledge in the beginning’. Meaning: the Upaniṣad, the Kārikā and Yoga share one story of where this knowledge came from.
1.26: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 69–70 trace Sāṃkhya to the supreme seer (paramarṣi) Kapila; Yoga places a teacher behind every teacher, outside time. Veda: Muṇḍaka Up. 1.1.1–2 — Brahmā taught Atharvan, who taught Aṅgir, and so on down the line. Meaning: the Veda presents knowledge as a chain; this sūtra names the first link.
1.27: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: Sāṃkhya has no mantra; Yoga takes this element straight from the Upaniṣads. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 1.2.15–17 — ‘the word all the Vedas proclaim … is Om; this syllable is Brahman, this is the best support’; Māṇḍūkya Up. 1 — ‘Om is all this.’ Ṛgveda 1.164.39 places the verses ‘in the imperishable syllable (akṣara) in the highest heaven.’ Meaning: Om is the Veda distilled into one sound.
1.28: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: repetition with meaning is the yogic form of SK 64’s ‘practice of the principles’. Veda: Muṇḍaka Up. 2.2.4 — ‘Om is the bow, the self is the arrow, Brahman the target; pierce it without carelessness and become one with it like the arrow’; Śvetāśvatara Up. 1.14 — make the body the lower fire-stick and Om the upper, and churn by meditation. Meaning: sound alone is not enough; the arrow must be aimed.
1.29: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: ‘pratyak-cetanā’, inward-turned consciousness, is the turn from the evolutes back toward puruṣa (SK 65). Veda: Kaṭha Up. 2.1.1 — ‘the Self-born pierced the senses outward … a wise one, seeking immortality, turned the eye inward and saw the inner Self (pratyag-ātman).’ Patañjali uses the Kaṭha’s own word. Meaning: Om turns the direction of attention around.
1.30: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 49 lists twenty-eight incapacities (aśakti) of the senses and intellect — Sāṃkhya’s catalogue of the same obstacles. Veda: Muṇḍaka Up. 2.2.4 — pierce ‘without carelessness (apramatta)’; carelessness (pramāda) is the fourth obstacle here. Meaning: the Veda’s warning against heedlessness becomes a checklist.
1.31: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 1 begins from the threefold suffering — bodily, mental and from outside; this sūtra shows them breaking into the practice itself. Veda: Śvetāśvatara Up. 2.13 lists the first signs of progress — lightness, health, steadiness, clear complexion, a pleasant voice; this sūtra lists the opposite. Meaning: body and breath are honest reports on the state of the mind.
1.32: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: Sāṃkhya’s one principle is the distinction itself (SK 37, 64); Yoga trains the mind on one object to make that possible. Veda: Chāndogya Up. 6.2.1 — ‘in the beginning this was Being alone, one without a second.’ Meaning: a mind trained on one thing can begin to see the One.
1.33: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: the four attitudes cultivate the sattvic dispositions of SK 23 (dharma, virāga). Veda: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 5.2 — the thunder says ‘da da da’: be restrained, give, be compassionate (dayadhvam); Īśa Up. 6 — one who sees all beings in the Self and the Self in all beings feels no aversion. Meaning: ethics here is a technique for a clear mind, not only a rule.
1.34: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 29 names the five breaths as the shared function of the inner instruments, so steadying breath steadies them. Veda: Śvetāśvatara Up. 2.9 — ‘restraining the breaths here, with movements controlled, breathe out through the nose when breath is spent’; Atharvaveda 11.4 praises Prāṇa, ‘in whose control is all this.’ Meaning: the breath is the handle the mind can be held by.
1.35: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: subtle sense-objects are the tanmātras of SK 38 — the non-specific objects behind sound, touch, form, taste and smell. Veda: Śvetāśvatara Up. 2.11 — fog, smoke, sun, wind, fire, fireflies, lightning, crystal, moon: forms that appear before Brahman in yoga. Meaning: early experiences of subtle perception build confidence and bind the mind.
1.36: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: the ‘luminous, sorrowless’ state is pure sattva, which SK 13 calls light (prakāśaka) and SK 12 pleasant. Veda: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 4.3.7 — ‘the person made of knowing, the light within the heart’; Chāndogya Up. 8.7.1 — the Self is ‘sorrowless’ (viśoka), the very word used here. Meaning: the Upaniṣad’s inner light becomes an object of meditation.
1.37: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 23 — dispassion (virāga) is a sattvic form of buddhi; resting the mind on one who has it lets it take that form. Veda: Muṇḍaka Up. 3.2.2 — one whose desires are fulfilled, whose self is made, ‘all desires dissolve here and now’; Kaṭha Up. 2.3.14 — ‘when all desires of the heart are released, the mortal becomes immortal.’ Meaning: we become like what we contemplate.
1.38: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: dream and sleep are vṛttis of buddhi (1.10), so they can be objects. Veda: Māṇḍūkya Up. 3–7 builds its whole teaching on waking, dream (taijasa), deep sleep (prājña), and the fourth that witnesses all three; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 4.3.9–14 — in dream ‘the person is his own light.’ Meaning: the states we pass through nightly are a training ground.
1.39: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: Sāṃkhya accepts that buddhi takes whatever form it is turned to (SK 23, 36); Yoga allows any congenial object. Veda: Chāndogya Up. 7 — Sanatkumāra leads Nārada through name, speech, mind, will and up, saying of each ‘meditate on it as Brahman.’ Meaning: begin wherever the mind can actually rest.
1.40: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: the range is from paramāṇu to the cosmic — the gross elements to mahat (SK 22, 38). Veda: Kaṭha Up. 1.2.20 and Śvetāśvatara Up. 3.20 — ‘smaller than the small, greater than the great, the Self is set in the cave of the heart.’ Meaning: a mind trained to stillness can hold the tiny and the vast alike.
1.41: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: the crystal image is Sāṃkhya’s standard picture of puruṣa and buddhi colouring each other (SK 20). Veda: Śvetāśvatara Up. 2.14 — ‘as a mirror stained with dust shines brightly when cleaned, so the embodied one, seeing the truth of the Self, becomes one’; Muṇḍaka Up. 2.2.4 — ‘become one with it like the arrow (tanmaya).’ Meaning: a clean mind takes the exact shape of what it meets.
1.42: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: word, meaning and idea are mixed — the vikalpa of 1.9; SK 28 says the senses only bare-present (ālocana), and the mixing is buddhi’s work. Veda: Chāndogya Up. 6.1.4 — ‘a modification is a name arising from speech; clay alone is real.’ Meaning: first absorption still carries labels.
1.43: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: when memory is purified the object shines alone — SK 28’s bare presentation (ālocanamātra). Veda: Chāndogya Up. 7.26.2 — ‘with pure sattva memory becomes firm’; Kena Up. 1.5–6 — what the mind cannot think, but by which the mind is thought. Meaning: seeing without naming.
1.44: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: subtle objects are the aviśeṣa — tanmātras and ahaṃkāra (SK 38). Veda: Chāndogya Up. 6.12 — the banyan seed: ‘this subtle essence you do not see, from it this great tree stands’. Meaning: the same practice now works on what lies behind the visible.
1.45: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: ‘up to the unmarked (aliṅga)’ is prakṛti itself, which SK 8 says is not seen because it is subtle, and SK 10 calls ‘without marks’. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 1.3.11 — ‘beyond the great is the unmanifest (avyakta), beyond the unmanifest the Person.’ Meaning: meditation can reach the root of nature, but the Person lies one step further.
1.46: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: ‘with seed’ because the object is still part of prakṛti; SK 21’s conjunction is not yet undone. Veda: Muṇḍaka Up. 1.1.4–5 — two knowledges, the lower (including the four Vedas) and the higher, ‘by which the imperishable is grasped.’ Meaning: even the highest absorption on an object is still the lower knowledge.
1.47: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: the ‘clarity of the inner self’ is buddhi at its most sattvic, the state SK 37 says alone can discern puruṣa. Veda: Muṇḍaka Up. 3.1.8 — ‘not by eye, not by speech … by the grace of knowledge, the pure in nature (viśuddha-sattva) sees him in meditation.’ Meaning: the Upaniṣad’s ‘pure sattva’ is the yogi’s goal here.
1.48: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 64’s ‘complete, pure, errorless knowledge’ is the ṛtaṃbharā prajñā. Veda: ‘ṛta’, cosmic truth-order, is one of the Ṛgveda’s central words; Taittirīya Up. 1.1 — ‘I shall speak ṛta, I shall speak satya.’ Meaning: the yogi’s insight is said to carry the same truth the Vedic seers named ṛta.
1.49: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: SK 4–6 rank perception above inference and testimony; here direct insight outranks both. Veda: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Up. 2.4.5 — hearing and reflecting lead to seeing; Kaṭha Up. 1.2.9 — ‘this insight is not reached by reasoning’; Chāndogya Up. 7.1.3 — Nārada knew the Vedas but not the Self. Meaning: scripture and reason point; insight sees the particular thing itself.
1.50: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: one saṃskāra blocks the others — like SK 67’s wheel slowly losing its old impetus. Veda: Muṇḍaka Up. 2.2.8 — ‘the knot of the heart is cut, all doubts dispelled, and his karmas wear out when that is seen.’ Meaning: true insight leaves an impression strong enough to crowd out the rest.
1.51: Sāṃkhya ↔ Yoga: seedless samādhi is SK 68’s final isolation in life: nothing left for prakṛti to show. Veda: Kaṭha Up. 2.3.10 — ‘when the intellect does not stir, that is the highest goal’; Māṇḍūkya Up. 7 — the fourth, ‘peaceful, auspicious, non-dual.’ Meaning: the practice ends where the Upaniṣads end — in a stillness that needs no object.
